newsitem.title: UK: Analysts lukewarm on Telewest, NTL.
newsitem.headline: Analysts lukewarm on Telewest, NTL.

text.p: British cable company Telewest Communications Plc confirmed on Monday that it was considering an approach by smaller rival NTL Inc, but some analysts warned against any merger.

Telewest, which is expected to report half-year pre-tax losses of around 145 million pounds ($236.4 million) on Thursday as it continues to roll out its network, said it had been approached by Nasdaq-listed NTL about two weeks ago.
But a spokesman stressed that any talks were at a very early stage.
"NTL is not exactly a glittering bride," said one telecoms analyst, however, who declined to be named.
He said debt-laden Telewest would do better signing a deal with Cable and Wireless Communications (CWC), Britain's biggest cable television and telephone company.
Increasing consolidation in the cable industry has already forced Telewest into second place and the group has been scouting around for cable and media partners in Britain and America.
"There has been an approach and we are looking at it as we look at any other approach," the Telewest spokesman said.
He declined to comment on the nature of the approach, but newspapers have said that NTL wants to merge with Telewest to create a 1.0 billion pound rival to CWC.

Telewest could also shed no light on newspaper reports that United News & Media Plc, the smallest of Britain's three big commercial television operators, might move into cable television by taking a minority stake in any new cable venture.
Both United News and NTL, which was formed after the acquisition of National Transcommunications Ltd by International CableTel in March 1996, declined to comment.
United, which had already established a close link with NTL, is still smarting from having seen its plans to boost its role in commercial television thwarted.

It had agreed to take a 30 pecent stake in a joint venture with NTL to bid for licences to operate multi-channel digital television in Britain. But it lost out in June to a rival consortium involving media giants Carlton Communications and Granada Group.

Telewest's shares, which have fallen from a 12-month high of 135p, rose four pence to 83p as some analysts noted that any NTL deal was unlikely to offer Telewest shareholders cash because of NTL's own heavy debts.
"It's bad news really," noted one analyst. "Telewest's management really owes it to its shareholders to cut a deal with CWC and cut the best deal it can -- I mean one pound-plus per share.
"I can only think that Telewest haven't struck a deal with CWC yet because the terms weren't very favourable. But I don't think they would get better terms from NTL."
Although Telewest and Cable and Wireless Communications have denied that they have held merger talks, they have said such a deal in the future is a possibility.
A deal with CWC would give the joint company access to over 10 million homes. Any deal with NTL will control franchises totalling around seven million homes.
Telewest has seen its shares suffer since it lost its top cable operator position in Britain to CWC, which joined the stock market in April following a complex four-way merger.
CWC brought together Cable and Wireless Plc's Mercury telephone subsidiary and the British cable TV units of NYNEX Corp and Bell Canada -- NYNEX CableComms Group Bell Cablemedia Plc and Videotron.
But because of the complexity of the merger, some analysts said that however keen CWC management was to add more partners, any imminent deal was unlikely.
"My gut feeling is that a Telewest and NTL deal has a higher chance of going ahead than any deal with CWC," said Andrew Moffatt, telecoms analyst at brokers SocGen.
"CWC has currently got a lot to digest." ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
